newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Key Colombian port hit by new labor problem.
newsitem.headline: Key Colombian port hit by new labor problem.

text.p: Truckers continued to prevent work from returning to normal in Colombia's main Pacific coast port of Buenaventura Friday afternoon, a day after dockworkers there lifted a crippling nine-day strike.

Port officials said the truck drivers, about 100 of them with big container rigs laden with coffee and other exports, were refusing to let their cargo be off-loaded onto awaiting ships until they received "standby" payments for time lost while the dockworkers were out on strike.
"It's a very complex problem," said one port official, who spoke on condition that he would not be identified.
He said the truckers were well within their rights to demand compensation for time and money lost while the port was shut down.
But private exporters were also well within their rights if they refused to compensate drivers for a problem they had nothing to do with, the port official said.

A Bogota-based spokeswoman for Colombian Truckers Association (ACC) said the drivers' sitdown strike was expected to continue at least through Saturday. The ACC, which is backing the job action, has called for payments of up to $3,000 for drivers adversely affected by the dockworkers' strike.
The ACC spokeswoman ruled out any link between the situation in Buenaventura and a possible nationwide truckers' strike next month.

ACC paralyzed coffee and other exports with an 11-day strike in October. It has vowed to stage another stoppage by the end of February if if fails to get a promised hike in freight rates in line with 1996 inflation of 21.63 percent.

Unless truckers let their rigs to be unloaded soon, coffee exporters face the likelihood of breaking December contracts and delivering late on January shipments. About 60 percent of Colombia's coffee shipments are handled threough Buenaventura.
